lessons.title: Why Companies Raise Money: Growth, Survival and Everything in Between

children.text: Your CEO walks into the quarterly town hall and announces: "We have raised ₹250 crore." People clap. Someone in sales assumes bonuses are coming. Someone in HR wonders if layoffs are off the table. Someone in finance quietly asks, "From whom, and on what terms?" All three reactions miss the first question that actually matters: why did the company need the money at all? This lesson answers that question, because every fundraising decision you will study in this course starts there.

body.text: Companies raise money when the cash they need to spend arrives before the cash they will earn. The reason for that gap decides how much to raise, how urgently, and from whom.

children.text: Every Business Spends Before It Earns

A bakery buys flour before it sells bread. A software company pays engineers for a year before the product earns a rupee. A cement maker spends three years building a plant before the first bag leaves the gate. The spending always comes first. The only question is how the business covers the gap.
The first and cheapest source is always the company's own cash, known as
internal accruals

. Profits that are not paid out as dividends stay in the business and fund the next round of spending. Mature, profitable Indian companies such as Asian Paints or TCS fund most of their needs this way. External fundraising begins only when internal cash is not enough, not fast enough, or both.

markDefs.definition: Cash a business generates from its own operations and keeps after paying expenses, taxes and dividends. It is the money a company can reinvest without asking anyone.

body.latex: \text{External funding needed} = \text{Cash required} - \text{Internal accruals} - \text{Surplus cash already held}
body.caption: Outside money fills only the gap that the business cannot fund itself

body.title: Size the gap
body.prompt: A Pune-based auto components maker plans ₹500 crore of spending on a new plant over the next two years. It expects to generate ₹320 crore of internal accruals in that period and already holds ₹30 crore of surplus cash. How much must it raise from outside, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹500 crore required, minus ₹320 crore of internal accruals, minus ₹30 crore of surplus cash, leaves ₹150 crore. That ₹150 crore is the number the company takes to banks or investors. Everything else it funds itself.

children.text: The Five Reasons Companies Raise Money
Strip away the press releases and almost every fundraise falls into one of five buckets. Learn to spot which one you are looking at, because each bucket points towards a different kind of money.

cells: Vodafone Idea's 2024 FPO earmarked the bulk of proceeds for 4G and 5G network equipment
Inventory, raw material and customer credit while waiting to be paid
A Tiruppur garment exporter funding a large European order until the buyer pays
Tata Steel's purchase of Anglo-Dutch steelmaker Corus in 2007
Reliance Industries raising money in 2020 to become net debt free
Staying solvent through losses or a crisis
Loss-making startups raising bridge rounds to extend their runway

children.text: Reason 1: Funding Growth
This is the reason founders love to talk about. The company has a way to grow that needs more
capital expenditure
than its profits can cover, so it brings in outside money to move faster than it could alone.

markDefs.definition: Money spent on long-lived assets such as factories, machinery, stores, towers or software platforms. Usually shortened to capex.

children.text: Zomato (now Eternal) is a clean example. Its July 2021 IPO, listed on NSE and BSE, raised ₹9,375 crore. But not all of that money went to Zomato.

stats.label: Offer for sale
stats.context: Info Edge sold shares, cash to Info Edge

children.text: The split matters. The
fresh issue
funded Zomato's growth plans. The
offer for sale
was simply an early investor cashing out part of its stake. When a headline says a company "raised" a large sum through an IPO, always check how much was fresh issue.

markDefs.definition: The part of an IPO or follow-on offer where the company creates and sells new shares. This money goes into the company's bank account.
The part of an IPO where existing shareholders sell their own shares to the public. The money goes to those sellers, not to the company.

body.text: Every Indian IPO document has a section called "Objects of the Issue" that lists exactly what the fresh issue money will be spent on. It is the most honest answer you will get to "why are they raising?", and it is legally binding on the company.

body.title: Where did the money go?
body.prompt: A consumer brand launches a ₹2,400 crore IPO on NSE and BSE. Of this, ₹1,500 crore is an offer for sale by its private equity investor. How much cash actually reaches the company, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Only the fresh issue reaches the company: ₹2,400 crore minus ₹1,500 crore of offer for sale leaves ₹900 crore. The other ₹1,500 crore goes to the selling investor. The company's headline IPO size is more than two and a half times what it actually receives.

children.text: Reason 2: Funding Working Capital
Here is a trap that catches profitable businesses every year: a company can be making money on every order and still run out of cash. The culprit is
working capital

markDefs.definition: The cash tied up in running day-to-day operations: raw material and inventory bought, plus money customers owe you, minus money you owe suppliers.

children.text: Kaveri Knits is a fictional garment exporter in Tiruppur. It holds ₹1 crore in the bank when it lands a ₹6 crore order from a European retailer. Yarn, dyeing and wages will cost ₹4.5 crore, paid in three equal monthly instalments of ₹1.5 crore while the garments are made. The buyer pays the full ₹6 crore only in month 5, after the goods are shipped and inspected. The order earns a healthy ₹1.5 crore profit. Now watch the bank balance.

body.title: Kaveri Knits: bank balance through the order (₹ crore)

children.text: By month 3 the balance would sit at minus ₹3.5 crore, and it stays there until the buyer pays. A bank account cannot go negative, so Kaveri Knits must arrange that ₹3.5 crore in advance, typically through a working capital loan or packing credit from its bank. Without it, the company cannot pay its suppliers, and a profitable order becomes a crisis.

body.title: Find the peak gap
body.prompt: Using the Kaveri Knits chart above, what is the maximum amount of outside funding the company needs at any single point during this order, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: The lowest balance is minus ₹3.5 crore in months 3 and 4: ₹1 crore at the start, less three payments of ₹1.5 crore. That trough is the funding requirement. Once the ₹6 crore arrives in month 5, the company can repay and still keep ₹2.5 crore, which is its starting ₹1 crore plus the ₹1.5 crore profit.

body.text: Growth makes this worse, not better. If Kaveri Knits wins three such orders at once, its peak gap roughly triples. Fast-growing businesses with long customer payment cycles are often the hungriest for working capital funding.

children.text: Reason 3: Buying Another Business
Some opportunities are too large and too sudden to fund from profits. When a company wants to buy another business, the money usually has to be arranged in weeks or months, not saved up over years.

body.label: Tata Steel's acquisition of Corus, 2007
body.context: Corus was several times larger than Tata Steel by production. The deal was funded with a mix of Tata Steel's own cash and large acquisition loans, with debt carrying the heaviest share. The burden of servicing that debt through the 2008 global downturn became a lesson in how acquisition funding can shape a company for a decade.

children.text: Reason 4: Fixing the Balance Sheet

Sometimes the money raised is not spent on anything new at all. It replaces or repays old borrowings. A company might refinance a loan at 11% with new money at 8.5%, or cut its borrowings sharply because lenders, rating agencies or shareholders are uncomfortable with how much it owes.
Reliance Industries did exactly this at enormous scale in 2020, bringing its
net debt
down to zero.

markDefs.definition: Total borrowings minus cash and liquid investments. A company with more cash than borrowings is net debt free.

body.title: How Reliance Industries became net debt free

events.title: The promise
events.description: At its AGM, Reliance commits to becoming net debt free by 31 March 2021.

events.title: Facebook invests
events.description: Facebook agrees to invest ₹43,574 crore for a 9.99% stake in Jio Platforms.

events.title: More stake sales
events.description: Global investors including Silver Lake, KKR, and sovereign funds from Saudi Arabia and the UAE buy stakes in Jio Platforms.

events.title: Rights issue
events.description: Reliance raises ₹53,124 crore from its own shareholders, then India's largest ever rights issue.

events.title: Target met early
events.description: Reliance declares itself net debt free, about nine months ahead of its own deadline.

body.text: Notice what Reliance used to repay debt: equity. It sold minority stakes in a subsidiary and issued new shares. Paying off one kind of capital by raising the other is one of the most common moves in corporate finance, and you will see it again in Chapter 4.

children.text: Reason 5: Survival

This is the reason nobody puts in a press release. The company is losing money, its existing cash is running out, and without new capital it cannot pay salaries, suppliers or lenders. For a startup, the key number is
runway

markDefs.definition: How many months a company can keep operating with the cash it has, at its current rate of spending, before it runs out.

children.text: Vodafone Idea's ₹18,000 crore follow-on public offer in April 2024, the largest FPO in Indian market history at the time, sat on the line between growth and survival. The stated use was network expansion. The underlying reality was a heavily indebted telecom operator that needed fresh equity to stay competitive against Jio and Airtel and to unlock further bank funding.

body.title: Raising from strength vs raising from weakness

columns.label: Raising from strength
points: Company can walk away if terms are poor
Several investors or lenders compete to fund it
Better valuation for equity, lower interest rate for debt

columns.label: Raising from weakness
points: Company must accept whatever is offered
Few willing funders, sometimes only existing ones
Lower valuation or higher interest rate
Tight conditions, extra security, board seats demanded
The bank balance chooses the timing

body.text: The best time to raise money is when you do not urgently need it. Treasury teams and experienced founders plan fundraises 12 to 18 months ahead for exactly this reason.

body.title: Name the reason
body.question: A listed hospital chain raises ₹800 crore and uses the entire amount to repay a term loan charging 11.5%, replacing it with nothing. Its expansion plans are unchanged. Which reason best describes this fundraise?
body.explanation: The money is not buying new hospitals or funding day-to-day operations. It is repaying existing borrowings, which is balance sheet repair. Nothing in the question suggests the company is in distress, so survival does not fit.

body.title: Read the signal
body.question: A profitable FMCG distributor with rising sales tells its bank it needs a larger credit limit because retailers now take 60 days to pay instead of 30. What is driving this funding need?
options: Survival, because the company is in trouble
Working capital, because more cash is stuck with customers
Growth capex, because sales are rising
body.explanation: Nothing is being built or bought. Doubling the credit period doubles the cash tied up in money owed by retailers, so the distributor needs more working capital funding even though the business is healthy.

body.title: The IPO trap
body.textWithBlank: In an IPO, money from the ___ goes to the company, while money from the offer for sale goes to the selling shareholders.
body.explanation: Only new shares created by the company bring cash into the business. An offer for sale transfers existing shares from one owner to another.

body.title: The town hall announcement
body.scenario: You work in the L&D team of a Bengaluru-based SaaS company with 900 employees. At a town hall, the CEO announces a ₹400 crore raise. The slide says only "Fuelling our next phase." Your team is being asked to prepare internal communication for managers, and managers are already fielding questions from anxious employees.
body.prompt: What questions would you want finance or leadership to answer before you draft that communication, and why does each one matter to employees?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Why did we raise: growth, acquisition, debt repayment or to extend runway? This decides whether the message is "we are expanding" or "we are stabilising", and employees will see through the wrong one.
2. Is this equity or debt? Equity changes who owns the company and matters for anyone holding ESOPs. Debt brings repayment obligations and lender conditions.
3. How much runway or growth does it buy? "This funds our plans for the next 24 months" is far more reassuring than a large rupee figure with no context.
4. What will the money actually be spent on: hiring, new markets, product, repaying loans? This tells managers whether headcount plans are changing.
5. Were any existing investors selling, or is all the money coming into the company? A large secondary component is a different story from fresh capital.
6. What can and cannot be shared externally? Especially important if the company plans to list later.

body.title: Decode any fundraise headline in five steps
steps: Find the total amount and who provided it
Separate money going to the company from money going to selling shareholders
Identify the stated reason: growth, working capital, acquisition, balance sheet or survival
Check whether the company raised from strength (profitable, choosing timing) or weakness (losses, urgent)
For listed companies, read the "Objects of the Issue" or the stock exchange filing on NSE or BSE

body.label: SEBI: Public Issues Filings
body.description: Browse draft and final offer documents for Indian IPOs and FPOs. Open any one and jump to "Objects of the Issue" to see exactly why the company is raising money.

body.title: Go deeper: why companies prefer internal cash first

children.text: Corporate finance has a well-known idea called the pecking order. Companies tend to fund themselves in a predictable sequence: first internal accruals, then debt, and only then new equity.
Internal cash
needs nobody's permission, costs no fees and reveals nothing to outsiders.
Debt
comes next because it does not reduce the owners' stake, and lenders ask fewer questions about the company's long-term prospects than equity investors do.
New equity
comes last because it dilutes existing owners, and outsiders often read a share sale as a sign that management thinks the shares are fully priced.

Real companies do not follow this order rigidly. Loss-making startups, for instance, usually cannot borrow at all and go straight to equity. But the pecking order explains a lot of what you will see in the rest of this course.

cards.definition: Cash a business generates and retains from its own operations. The first and cheapest funding source.
Capital expenditure: spending on long-lived assets like plants, stores and networks.
Cash tied up in inventory and customer credit, less what the business owes suppliers.
New shares sold by the company. The cash goes into the company.
Existing shareholders selling their shares. The cash goes to the sellers.
Total borrowings minus cash and liquid investments.
Months a company can operate on its current cash at its current burn rate.
The section of an Indian offer document stating exactly how fresh issue proceeds will be used.

points: Companies raise external money only to cover the gap between cash required and cash they generate or already hold.
Almost every fundraise fits one of five reasons: growth capex, working capital, acquisitions, fixing the balance sheet or survival.
A profitable business can still run short of cash when it pays suppliers long before customers pay it.
In an IPO, only the fresh issue funds the company. The offer for sale goes to selling shareholders.
Raising from strength gets better terms than raising from weakness, so good companies raise before they are desperate.
The reason for raising shapes the right type of money, which is where the rest of this course goes next.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Knits and other unnamed companies are fictional illustrations. Figures for real companies are drawn from public disclosures and news reports at the time of each event and are rounded for clarity.
